details:
**Harold Godwinson**
The last Anglo-Saxon king of England, who took the throne after Edward the Confessor died in January 1066. He lost and was killed at Hastings on October 14, 1066, ending Anglo-Saxon rule; his brothers Gyrth and Leofwine also died in the battle.

**William the Conqueror**
The Duke of Normandy who claimed the English throne, invaded, and won at Hastings, beginning the Norman Conquest. He was crowned King of England in Westminster Abbey on Christmas Day 1066, when his nervous troops mistook the cheers of acclamation for a riot and set fire to nearby buildings.

**Bayeux Tapestry**
A roughly 70-meter embroidered cloth (technically an embroidery, not a true tapestry) narrating the events leading up to the conquest and culminating in the battle. It was probably commissioned by William's half-brother Bishop Odo of Bayeux, Earl of Kent, and it includes one of the earliest depictions of Halley's Comet.

**Arrow in the eye**
The famous tradition that Harold was killed by an arrow to the eye, based on a figure in the Bayeux Tapestry. Historians debate whether the figure is Harold and whether the story is true, since early accounts such as William of Poitiers' give few clear details of his death.

**Battle of Stamford Bridge**
Fought on the River Derwent near York less than three weeks before Hastings. Harold defeated the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada and Harold's own exiled brother Tostig, both of whom were killed. He then had to force-march his weakened army south to face William.

**Senlac Hill**
The ridge where Harold's army took its defensive position, giving the battle the alternate name "Battle of Senlac." The English had camped the night before on nearby Caldbec Hill at a landmark called the "hoar apple tree."

**Housecarls, fyrd, and the shield wall**
Harold's army combined housecarls, his elite professional bodyguard troops, with the fyrd, a militia of local freemen. They formed a dense shield wall on the hilltop that held for much of the day against Norman archers, infantry, and cavalry.

**Feigned retreat**
After Breton troops on William's left wing broke and fled, pursued by English fyrdmen, the Norman knights turned and cut down the pursuers. They then deliberately staged fake retreats to lure more defenders off the hill, weakening the shield wall.

**Pevensey**
The place on the Sussex coast where William's invasion fleet landed in late September 1066, before he moved to Hastings. The fleet had earlier waited at the mouth of the Dives River in Normandy for favorable winds.

**Malfosse ("Evil Ditch")**
A ditch where retreating English soldiers made a last stand at the end of the battle, ambushing and inflicting heavy losses on pursuing Normans. Eustace II, Count of Boulogne, was wounded there and may have ordered a retreat.

**Taillefer**
A Norman jester or minstrel who, according to legend, began the battle by riding out alone toward the English lines while reciting the Song of Roland. He was said to have killed the first English soldier before being killed himself.

**Battle Abbey**
An abbey William founded on the battlefield itself, reportedly with its high altar placed where Harold fell. It was built as penance for the bloodshed of the conquest; the town of Battle grew up around it.

**Harrying of the North**
William's brutal campaign of 1069–70, launched after the battle, that devastated the lands north of the River Humber to crush rebellions. Mass burning of crops and livestock led to widespread famine.

**Edward the Confessor's succession crisis**
Edward died childless in 1066, leaving rival claims from Harold (chosen by the Witan), William (who said Edward had promised him the throne), and Harald Hardrada (who cited an agreement between Magnus the Good and Harthacnut). Pope Alexander II backed William's invasion.

**Alan Rufus and the "Proven Companions"**
Alan Rufus ("Alan the Red"), a Breton nobleman, commanded the Breton troops and was later rewarded with the Honour of Richmond. The "Proven Companions" are about fifteen men, including Eustace of Boulogne, Walter Giffard, and Raoul II of Tosny, who are reliably documented as fighting for William.
